lead: Speech starts as air pushed out of the lungs. The vocal folds chop that air into pulses, and the throat and mouth shape the pulses into sounds. Engineers model this as a source signal driving a slowly changing filter. Sampled at 8 kHz or 16 kHz and cut into 20–30 ms frames, speech becomes a stream of numbers. Every speech recogniser, synthesiser and codec in this unit starts from this model.
prereq: You only need to know that a signal sampled at regular instants can be stored as a list of numbers.

sections.h3: Air, folds and cavities: how the body makes speech

blocks.text: Speech begins with breathing out. The lungs push air up the trachea, the windpipe. At the top sits the larynx, or voice box, holding the vocal folds — two small folds of tissue. When the folds are pulled together, air pressure builds until they are forced apart; the pressure drops, they close, and the cycle repeats. Each opening releases a small puff of air. This periodic pulsing is voiced excitation.

The pulsing rate is the fundamental frequency F0, in hertz (cycles per second). A typical adult male voice has F0 near 100–150 Hz; a typical adult female voice near 180–250 Hz. A pulse train repeating F0 times per second carries energy at F0 and at the whole-number multiples 2F0, 3F0 and so on. These multiples are the harmonics. When the folds are held apart the air stream is not pulsed, and the sound is unvoiced. The noise comes from turbulent air forced through a narrow constriction: at the glottis for /h/, and in the mouth for /s/ and /f/. In the source-filter model this unvoiced source is still fed into the same tract filter.

Above the larynx the air passes the pharynx (throat) and the oral cavity (mouth); when the soft palate is lowered it also enters the nasal cavity (nose). It leaves through the lips for oral sounds, and through the nose as well when the soft palate is lowered, as in /m/, /n/ and /ng/. These cavities act as resonators — they boost some frequencies and damp others. Move the tongue or the lips and the shape changes, so a different set of frequencies is boosted. That is why one pitch can carry many different vowels.

The source-filter model splits the work in two. The source e[n] is the excitation from the vocal folds: a pulse train for voiced sounds, noise for unvoiced ones. The filter h[n] is the vocal tract's impulse response, the output it would give for one puff of air. Real speech is the source shaped by the filter, so the sampled signal is their convolution:

blocks.where: x[n] is sample n of the recorded speech; e[k] is the k-th excitation sample; h[n − k] is the filter response to a puff k samples earlier; the sum runs over all past samples.

blocks.text: Source and filter are roughly independent. Hum a vowel low and then high: the pitch changes, the vowel does not, because the source changed while the filter stayed. The lips radiate the result into the air and add a mild high-frequency boost, which most implementations fold into the source. Some syllabi call e[n] the glottal source and H(z) the vocal tract transfer function.
The tract behaves like a tube, and a tube is well modelled by an all-pole filter:
H(z) = 1 / (1 − Σₖ aₖ z⁻ᵏ),  k = 1 to p
blocks.where: H(z) is the filter transfer function; aₖ are the filter coefficients; z⁻ᵏ is a delay of k samples; p is the filter order.

blocks.text: The poles of H(z) are the tract resonances, called formants. The usual order is p ≈ 10 at a sampling rate of 8 kHz and p ≈ 18 at 16 kHz, roughly one pole per kilohertz plus a few. Linear predictive coding (LPC) estimates the aₖ from one frame of speech. Section 7.3 turns these coefficients into a visible spectrum.

sections.h3: Sampling and frames: from air to numbers

blocks.text: A microphone converts air pressure into a voltage, and an analog-to-digital converter samples that voltage fs times per second. Speech is normally stored as 8 kHz or 16 kHz, 16-bit PCM. At 8 kHz the highest frequency that can be represented is 4 kHz, enough for telephone speech; 16 kHz keeps a wider band and is common in modern systems. In 16-bit PCM each sample is an integer from −32768 to 32767, so 65536 levels exist.

The tract cannot change shape instantly: the tongue and jaw have mass. Over about 20–30 ms the filter is nearly constant. This property is quasi-stationarity, and it licenses framing — cut the signal into short overlapping blocks and treat each block as if a fixed filter produced it. A 25 ms frame taken every 10 ms is a common choice, so neighbouring frames overlap by 15 ms.
With N samples in total, frame length L samples and hop S samples, frames start at 0, S, 2S and so on, and each must fit inside the signal:

blocks.where: N is the total number of samples; L is the frame length in samples; S is the frame shift (hop) in samples; floor rounds down to a whole number.

blocks.text: Frame rate is fs/S frames per second, set by the hop and not by the frame length. Many toolkits pad the tail instead of dropping it and report one extra frame.

examples.question: A 2-second mono recording is made at a sampling rate of 16 kHz with 16-bit PCM samples. (a) How many samples does it contain? (b) How many bits and how many bytes of raw storage does it need? (c) The signal is cut into frames of 25 ms with a hop of 10 ms. Give the frame length and hop in samples, and the number of frames.
steps: Number of samples = fs × duration = 16000 samples/s × 2 s = 32000 samples.
Number of bits = 32000 samples × 16 bits/sample = 512000 bits.
Number of bytes = 512000 ÷ 8 = 64000 bytes, that is 64 kB.
Number of frames = floor((N − L)/S) + 1 = floor((32000 − 400)/160) + 1 = floor(31600/160) + 1 = floor(197.5) + 1 = 197 + 1 = 198 frames.
examples.answer: 32000 samples, 512000 bits = 64000 bytes (64 kB) of storage, a 400-sample frame with a 160-sample hop, and 198 frames.
examples.check:
fs = 16000
duration_s = 2
bits_per_sample = 16
frame_ms = 25
hop_ms = 10
N = fs * duration_s
bits = N * bits_per_sample
bytes_total = bits // 8
L = frame_ms * fs // 1000
S = hop_ms * fs // 1000
frames = (N - L) // S + 1
print(N)
print(bits)
print(bytes_total)
print(L)
print(S)
print(frames)

traps: Mixing up sampling rate and frame rate. 16 kHz is samples per second; the frame rate is fs/hop = 16000/160 = 100 frames per second.
Thinking F0 is the sampling rate. A male F0 is 100–150 Hz and a female F0 is 180–250 Hz, while fs is 8000 or 16000 Hz.
Using the frame length as the step. A 25 ms frame with a 10 ms hop overlaps by 15 ms; the hop fixes the frame rate.
Dropping the +1 in the frame count, or using ceil((N − L)/S) instead of floor((N − L)/S) + 1.
Swapping source and filter. F0 and its harmonics belong to the source; formants belong to the filter.

quiz.q: Name the two blocks of the source-filter model and say what each one represents.
quiz.a: The source e[n] is the vocal-fold excitation: a pulse train for voiced sounds, noise for unvoiced ones. The filter h[n] is the vocal tract impulse response, fixed by the shape of the throat, mouth and nose.

quiz.q: Define quasi-stationarity and give the frame length it allows.
quiz.a: The vocal tract changes slowly enough that over 20–30 ms its filter is nearly constant, so frames of about 25 ms can be treated as stationary.

quiz.q: Why does a vowel keep its identity when it is sung at a much higher pitch?
quiz.a: Pitch is F0, a property of the source. The vowel identity comes from the formants, the poles of the tract filter, and the tract shape has not changed. Only e[n] changed.

quiz.q: A 3-second mono recording is stored at 8 kHz with 16-bit PCM. Find the number of samples and the storage in bytes. Then find the frame length, hop and frame count for 25 ms frames with a 10 ms hop.
An LPC analysis is to be run on 16 kHz speech. Suggest a filter order and justify it.
quiz.a: p ≈ 18. The rule is about one pole per kilohertz of bandwidth plus a few extra, so 16 kHz needs about 18 while 8 kHz needs about 10.

quiz.q: A student writes: "For a male speaker, F0 = 16000 Hz." Correct the statement, and state what 16000 Hz really is and what the frame rate is for a 25 ms frame with a 10 ms hop.
quiz.a: F0 for a male speaker is near 100–150 Hz, not 16000 Hz. 16000 Hz is the sampling rate fs. The frame rate is fs/hop = 16000/160 = 100 frames per second.

quiz.q: Two recordings of the same sentence differ in pitch, yet their LPC coefficients match frame by frame. Explain why both facts can hold.
quiz.a: LPC coefficients describe only the filter, that is the tract shape. The pitch difference means a different source e[n], with a different F0 and harmonic spacing, which lies outside the all-pole filter. The same words move the tract the same way, so the aₖ agree.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the source-filter view is the basis of every speech codec: the LPC and CELP families used in mobile calls send filter coefficients plus a coded excitation instead of raw samples. Neural vocoders keep the same split, with a network predicting a spectral envelope and a separate source supplying pulses or noise. Search for linear predictive coding, source-filter model of speech, and neural vocoder to go further.
